Two things in this subject are true with no caveats at all, and everything else is a corollary of them.

**A graph is exactly the set of points whose coordinates satisfy the equation.** Not a picture *of* the equation — the equation's solution set, drawn. So a drawing is correct exactly when every point on it satisfies the equation, and a point is on the curve exactly when the numbers work. This is the ground your paper work was standing on loosely: your numbers were right and your placement was judged by eye instead of by substitution.

**A square is never negative, and it is zero only at zero.** $t^2\ge 0$, with $t^2=0$ only when $t=0$.

Put those together and the vertex form decomposes with nothing left over:

$$y-k=a(x-h)^2 \quad\text{means}\quad \text{vertical offset from } k \;=\; a\cdot(\text{horizontal distance from } x=h)^2$$

Everything you want to know about the graph is a consequence of that one sentence. The extreme point is forced by the square being smallest at zero. The axis is forced because squaring erases the sign of the distance. Stepping $t$ to either side of the axis must land at the same height, $k+at^2$ — the symmetry is not a rule about parabolas, it is what squaring *does*. Width is what $a$ does to that rise per step. And the intercepts are just the steps that happen to bring the height to zero.

So the arc does not re-teach you $h$, $k$, and $a$ — you already read those correctly. It goes: definition of a graph → the square forces the vertex → the distance-to-height ladder → $a$ sets the rise per step (which settles the $0<|a|<1$ case you haven't been tested on, by derivation rather than by memory) → the one place your hands lag your head, plotting on a fixed uniform scale → the inverse directions: reading $(a,h,k)$ back off a graph, and manufacturing vertex form out of standard form, which gets a *reason* here rather than a ritual → the root count as the payoff, so the form answers graph questions with no drawing at all.
